title: Reading the coach: short commands and signals
summary: On the stand a coach speaks in fragments and gestures. What the short words and common hand signals mean, and how to answer the coach’s questions.

body.html: On the stand a coach speaks in fragments: “Behind.” “Head.” “More.” “Again.” There are only a few seconds between targets, so the short words are deliberate. Each one points to a single thing to change or to keep.
Many fragments say where the shot went: behind, in front, over or under the target. Others name what to fix: “head” means keep your cheek on the stock, and “feet” means check your stance.

Many coaches ask before they tell: “Where did it go?” or “What did you see?” This is a teaching question, not a test. Answer with what you really saw, even if you are not sure: “I think behind” or “I lost it at the end”. The coach needs your picture (what you saw at the shot) to find the cause.

Hand signals carry a lot. Hands moving apart or together usually mean more or less lead. A flat hand moving down means “lower”, and a tap on the cheek means “head down on the stock”. A finger may trace the target’s line, and a thumbs-up means “same again”. Signals differ between coaches, so agree on them before the session.

Some words are rhythm and encouragement rather than technique: “commit”, “trust it”, “smooth”, “good, same again”. “Bad luck” after a miss is kindness, not a comment on the referee. More phrases like these: The mental game in coach-speak.

In competition coaching is forbidden: the referee gives the competitor a yellow card and sends the coach out of the shooting area (Chapter 8 · No coaching during competition, Chapter 21 · No coaching during competition). So all this coach language belongs to training. The rules do not say whether an interpreter may relay a coach’s advice during a competition. The safe practice is to interpret only for the referee, the jury and the organiser.

notes.html: Translate the coach’s question, let the shooter answer, and translate the answer back exactly, even if it sounds wrong. Keep your words as short as the coach’s: a long sentence arrives after the next call.
Do not translate a gesture the shooter has already seen. Keep the coach’s tone: encouragement stays warm, and safety stays firm.

key_points.html: Coaches speak in fragments; each word points to one thing to change or keep.
“Where did it go?” is a teaching question: answer with what you really saw.
Agree on hand signals before the session.
No coaching in competition; interpret only for the referee, jury and organiser.

quiz.q: The coach asks the shooter “Where did it go?”. What should the interpreter do?

options.text: Translate the question, then the shooter’s answer exactly
Explain the miss in your own words
Say nothing: it is a rhetorical question

quiz.explain: The coach wants to hear what the shooter actually saw, so the answer must reach him unchanged.

quiz.q: During a competition the shooter’s coach asks you to pass on: “Give the next one more lead.” What is the safe practice?

options.text: Pass it on quietly, in a whisper
Pass it on, but only between stands
Decline: coaching is not allowed in competition

quiz.explain: Coaching in competition is forbidden, and the rules do not say whether an interpreter may relay it; staying out of it protects the shooter.

quiz.q: What do the rules say happens if the referee judges that a competitor is being coached?

options.text: Yellow card; the coach is sent away

quiz.explain: Both rulebooks give the competitor a yellow card, with heavier penalties for repeats, and the referee removes the coach from the shooting area.
